title: The Analytics Lifecycle and Data-Driven Decision Making
learning_objective: Describe the six stages of the analytics lifecycle in order, from a vague business concern to a communicated insight, and correctly identify which single stage a given real work task belongs to.
description_for_ai: The analytics lifecycle is a repeatable, six-stage loop, not a one-way line: Business Question, Data Collection, Data Preparation, Analysis, Interpretation, and Communication. Business Question turns a vague concern ("deliveries are late") into something specific and measurable ("what proportion of Ikeja deliveries in the last 30 days exceeded a 2-day delay?"). Data Collection identifies and gathers the data needed to answer it, such as a delivery log with columns order_id, dispatch_date, delivery_date, branch, and delay_days. Data Preparation cleans that raw data before any calculation, for example removing duplicate order_id rows, fixing impossible future dates, and standardising inconsistent branch-name casing ("ikeja" vs "Ikeja" vs " IKEJA"). Analysis applies a calculation to the prepared data, such as computing average delay_days per branch (Ikeja 2.3 days, Lekki 1.1 days, Yaba 0.9 days). Interpretation is the distinct step of stating what that number means for the business ("Ikeja's delay is nearly double every other branch and is driving most of this month's complaints"), which is not the same step as producing the chart itself. Communication presents the finding, the evidence, and a recommended next step to the person who can act on it (a one-slide summary to an operations manager recommending a dispatch-process review for Ikeja). The loop closes rather than stopping at Communication, because a recommendation like "investigate Ikeja's dispatch process" becomes the next cycle's Business Question.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Students jump straight to Data Collection or Analysis without first sharpening a vague concern into a specific, measurable Business Question, which makes it impossible to know when the task is answered. Students confuse Analysis with Interpretation, treating a finished chart or average as the end product instead of recognising that a sentence connecting the number to a business cause and consequence is a separate, required step. Students misclassify a Data Preparation task (removing duplicates, fixing casing, correcting impossible dates) as part of Analysis because both happen in the spreadsheet. Students describe the lifecycle as a single one-way sequence that ends at Communication, missing that a recommendation typically becomes the next Business Question, restarting the loop. Students treat every stage as equally time-consuming, when Data Preparation is typically the longest and most error-prone stage in practice.
example_code_for_ai:
# Business Question: Which branch has the worst delivery delays, and by how much?
# Data Collection: pull delivery_log.csv (order_id, dispatch_date, delivery_date, branch, delay_days), 400 rows, 3 branches
# Data Preparation: remove 12 duplicate order_id rows; fix 2 impossible future delivery dates; standardise branch casing
# Analysis: average(delay_days) grouped by branch -> Ikeja 2.3, Lekki 1.1, Yaba 0.9
# Interpretation: Ikeja's average delay is nearly double every other branch and is driving most complaints this month
# Communication: one-slide recommendation to the operations manager -> review Ikeja's dispatch process
# (this recommendation becomes the NEXT cycle's Business Question, closing the loop)

title: Data Types, Data Structures and the Data Team
learning_objective: Identify the four main data types in a dataset (numerical, categorical, date/time, text), distinguish structured from unstructured data, and describe where the data analyst sits among the roles on a data team.
description_for_ai: A data type describes the kind of value a column holds and what operations are meaningful on it. Numerical data is a measurable quantity, such as delay_days or order_value_naira, and can be averaged or summed. Categorical data places a record into one of a limited set of groups: branch (Ikeja, Lekki, Yaba) and delivery_partner are nominal (no natural order), while a column like customer_rating (1 to 5 stars) is ordinal (has a natural order); categorical data is counted or grouped, never averaged in the way a true quantity is. Date/time data such as dispatch_date and delivery_date supports duration calculations (delivery_date minus dispatch_date) and grouping by week or month. Text data such as complaint_notes is free-form and cannot be averaged or neatly grouped. A column made only of digits is not automatically numerical: order_id looks numerical but is really an identifier, a categorical field, because summing or averaging two order IDs is meaningless. Structured data fits neatly into a fixed set of rows and columns (a CSV like delivery_log.csv); unstructured data has no fixed shape (photos, emails, free text), and a text column like complaint_notes can hold unstructured content even while sitting inside an otherwise structured file. On a data team, the data engineer builds and maintains the pipelines that collect and store data, the data analyst cleans, explores, and interprets data to answer business questions and communicate findings, the data scientist builds predictive models and deeper statistical work, the BI developer builds and maintains recurring dashboards, and a data governance or protection officer sets rules for how data may be used; the analyst typically sits downstream of the engineer and upstream of the decision-maker.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Students classify order_id as numerical because it is made of digits, without checking whether averaging or summing it would be meaningful. Students treat an ordinal categorical column (customer_rating) the same as a nominal categorical column (branch), missing that ordinal data has a natural order. Students assume that because one column in a file (complaint_notes) is unstructured text, the entire file must be classified as unstructured, rather than recognising the file overall as structured. Students describe the data analyst and data scientist roles as interchangeable, missing that the analyst's core focus is answering business questions and communicating findings, while the data scientist goes further into predictive modelling.
example_code_for_ai:
# order_id -> categorical (identifier), NOT numerical, despite being digits
# dispatch_date, delivery_date -> date/time
# branch, delivery_partner -> categorical (nominal)
# delay_days, order_value_naira -> numerical
# complaint_notes -> text, unstructured content inside a structured file
# Overall file (delivery_log.csv) -> structured, because every record shares the same fixed columns
# Data team: Data Engineer -> Data Analyst (this role) -> Decision-maker, with Data Scientist and BI Developer alongside

title: The AI-Augmented Analyst and Toolkit Setup
learning_objective: Set up and navigate the programme's AI toolkit (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Google Colab, and publica.academy), and describe what changes and what does not change about the analyst's job when AI tools are introduced.
description_for_ai: The programme toolkit has five components. Claude and ChatGPT are chat-based assistants suited to structured reasoning, drafting, and exploring an unfamiliar dataset quickly. Gemini is tightly integrated with Google's own tools, useful when work already lives in Sheets or Docs. Google Colab is not a chat assistant but a free, browser-based notebook for running real code, used from later modules onward. publica.academy is the home base for downloads, quizzes, and progress tracking. Setting up the toolkit means creating or confirming accounts on all three assistants with the same registered email, confirming a new Google Colab notebook can be created, and locating the current module's downloads on publica.academy. What changes when AI tools are used: drafting speed, first-pass code or formulas, and summarising or exploring data quickly. What does not change: the analyst still owns the business question, still judges whether an answer makes sense, and still verifies before anyone else sees the work. A concrete illustration: pasting a currency column such as order_value_naira into an assistant as plain text, with symbols and commas left in, and asking for the total, can produce a confidently stated but incorrect total that only matches the real spreadsheet SUM once checked; this is the exact reason verification is treated as non-negotiable from the first time AI tools are used.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Students accept an AI assistant's first answer to a calculation task without comparing it against a manual or spreadsheet result, especially for something that looks simple, like a total or a count. Students believe AI tools remove the need to define a precise business question, rather than recognising the question still has to come from the analyst. Students pick an assistant based on general brand preference rather than fit for the task at hand (for example, using Gemini for work that already lives in Google Sheets). Students assume a wrong AI answer means the tool is broken, rather than recognising that pasted currency symbols, commas, or ambiguous formatting are a common, specific cause of a miscalculated total.
example_code_for_ai:
# Setup checklist:
# 1. Confirm accounts on Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini (same registered email)
# 2. Open Google Colab and create a blank notebook
# 3. Log in to publica.academy and locate this week's downloads
#
# Hook exercise:
# Paste order_value_naira column as plain text (with currency symbols/commas) into an assistant, ask for the total
# Compare assistant's stated total against spreadsheet SUM(order_value_naira)
# If they mismatch: this demonstrates why every AI answer must be verified, not trusted on confidence alone

title: Prompt Fundamentals for Data Work
learning_objective: Write a prompt that gives an AI assistant context, a data description, a task, and an output format, and iterate on a prompt that returns a poor first answer by diagnosing and sharpening one ingredient at a time.
description_for_ai: A strong data prompt combines four ingredients. Context is one sentence stating the role or situation, such as "You are helping a Lagos logistics firm understand why deliveries are running late." Data description tells the assistant what the dataset actually contains, since it usually cannot see the spreadsheet directly, for example "Here is a delivery log with columns order_id, dispatch_date, delivery_date, branch, and delay_days, 400 rows across three branches." Task states precisely what should be done, matching the same precision used for a Business Question, for example "Calculate the average delay_days per branch and identify the branch with the highest average" rather than the vague "Look at the delays." Output format states exactly how the answer should be structured, for example "Return the result as a table with columns branch and average_delay_days, sorted from highest to lowest," which avoids an unstructured paragraph that needs manual reformatting. A poor first answer is expected and normal: the correct response is to diagnose which single ingredient was thin or missing, not to abandon the prompt or assume the task is impossible. A real three-step iteration: Iteration 1 ("What's wrong with my delivery data?") has no data description, task, or format and returns a generic answer; Iteration 2 adds data description and task ("Here is a delivery log with columns order_id, dispatch_date, delivery_date, branch, delay_days, 400 rows. Find rows where delay_days does not match delivery_date minus dispatch_date.") but still returns a long paragraph; Iteration 3 adds output format ("Return any mismatches as a table with columns order_id, expected_delay, and actual_delay") and produces a clean, checkable table, which is then still verified by manually recalculating one flagged row.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Students write a task that is too vague ("Look at the delays") without stating exactly what calculation or comparison is wanted, mirroring the same weakness a poorly sharpened Business Question has. Students omit the data description and are then surprised when the assistant misreads a column, for example miscounting a currency total because it was not told the column contains symbols or commas. Students omit an output format and then manually reformat a long paragraph by hand instead of simply asking for a table in the first prompt. Students treat a poor first answer as proof the task cannot be done by AI, instead of diagnosing which single ingredient was thin and revising only that one. Students skip verifying the final, well-formatted answer, assuming that a clean table is automatically a correct one.
example_code_for_ai:
# Iteration 1: "What's wrong with my delivery data?"
# -> no context, no data description, no task, no format: generic, unusable answer
#
# Iteration 2: "Here is a delivery log with columns order_id, dispatch_date, delivery_date, branch,
# delay_days, 400 rows. Find rows where delay_days does not match delivery_date minus dispatch_date."
# -> data description + task added: better, but returns a long unstructured paragraph
#
# Iteration 3: "...Return any mismatches as a table with columns order_id, expected_delay, actual_delay."
# -> output format added: clean, checkable table
# Verification: manually recalculate one flagged row before trusting the rest

title: Verification Habits and Responsible Use
learning_objective: Verify an AI-produced answer against a known result using recalculation, spot-checking, or cross-referencing; list the categories of data that must never be entered into an AI tool; and explain in outline why Nigerian data protection law makes this a professional duty.
description_for_ai: Verification means checking an AI-produced answer against something trusted more than the assistant's confidence; "it looks right" is explicitly not verification. Three named methods: recalculate (redo the same calculation independently, by hand or with a formula, and compare), spot-check (pick a small sample of rows or results and confirm each manually), and cross-reference (compare the answer against a separate, already-trusted source, such as an earlier report). The method should match the stakes: a low-effort, high-stakes number such as "Ikeja's average delay is 2.3 days, the highest of the three branches" warrants a full recalculation before it drives a business recommendation. Certain categories of data must never be entered into any AI tool: real customer names, phone numbers, or addresses; real payment or account details; real colleague, employer, or client confidential information; and any dataset containing real identifiable people, even in a single column. delivery_log.csv is safe to use throughout the programme specifically because these categories were removed or replaced with generated values before distribution, not because the file is small or used only internally. The Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) governs how personal data may be collected, stored, and processed, and pasting a customer's real details into a public AI tool can count as an unauthorised transfer of personal data to a third party; this makes safe data handling a professional duty resting with the individual analyst in the moment of use, not only with an employer's written policy, since analysts routinely handle the personal data that other roles collect. When asked to paste real, identifying data into an AI tool, the correct response is to decline, explain the specific category of data present, and propose an alternative such as removing or replacing identifying columns first.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Students accept an AI-produced answer because it "looks right" or is stated confidently, instead of applying one of the three named verification methods. Students verify a claim once and assume every subsequent claim from the same assistant is automatically trustworthy without rechecking. Students believe that removing only the most obviously sensitive field (for example, phone numbers but not names) makes a dataset safe to paste, rather than recognising that any category of real personal data, even one column, is enough to make a file unsafe. Students describe data protection as solely the employer's responsibility or the IT department's policy, missing that the professional duty rests with whichever individual is handling the data at that moment.
example_code_for_ai:
# Claim: "Ikeja's average delay is 2.3 days, the highest of the three branches."
# Verification method chosen: recalculate (low-effort, high-stakes number)
# AVERAGEIF(branch_range, "Ikeja", delay_range) -> 2.3 -> matches claim -> now safe to communicate
#
# Never paste checklist:
# - real customer names, phone numbers, addresses
# - real payment or account details
# - real colleague/employer/client confidential data
# delivery_log.csv is safe: identifying columns were removed/generated before distribution
